lessons.title: How MIG Works on Aluminium
lessons.body: MIG welding aluminium uses a continuous wire electrode fed through a gun, with argon shielding gas. The wire melts into the joint, forming a weld. Unlike steel, aluminium conducts heat away fast and melts at about 660Â°C, so you need higher heat input and faster travel speeds. The wire is softer and can tangle easily, so a spool gun or push-pull system helps. In Africa, many workshops use portable MIG sets like the Telwin or Deca, often powered by a generator. Set your machine to DCEP (electrode positive) for best penetration. Use a contact tip slightly larger than the wire, e.g., 1.2mm tip for 1.0mm wire, to avoid binding. Keep your stick-out about 10-15mm. Push the gun away from the weld pool (forehand) to get good cleaning action from the argon. Argon gas flow should be 12-18 litres per minute. If you hear a popping sound, your wire feed or gas flow is off. Clean the aluminium with a stainless steel brush before welding to remove oxide. Practice on 3mm thick 6061 plates. Set voltage around 20-22V and wire speed to match. Listen for a steady sizzling sound like frying bacon. If the wire stubs into the plate, increase voltage or reduce wire speed. If the wire balls up, reduce voltage or increase wire speed. Keep a consistent travel angle of 10-15 degrees. For a 3mm fillet weld, use about 120-150 amps. Remember, aluminium has no colour change when hot, so use a good helmet with a clear lens. Always wear leather gloves and a respirator; aluminium oxide fumes are harmful. In rural areas, ensure your generator can supply at least 5kVA for a 200A MIG set. Practice on scrap until you get a smooth, rippled bead without burn-through.

lessons.title: Spool Guns and Push-Pull Systems
lessons.body: Aluminium wire is soft and can buckle when pushed through a standard MIG torch. That's why spool guns and push-pull systems exist. A spool gun has a small spool of wire mounted directly on the gun, so the wire only travels a short distance. This eliminates feeding problems. Spool guns are common in African workshops because they are cheaper than push-pull systems. A typical spool gun like the Miller Spoolmate 100 or a generic 200A model costs around $200-$400. They work well for short welds and repairs. However, the spool is small (usually 0.5kg or 1kg), so you refill often. For longer production runs, a push-pull system is better. It has a torch with a small motor in the handle that pulls the wire, while the main feeder pushes. This allows using a standard 15kg spool on the machine. Push-pull torches like the Binzel or Tregaskiss are more expensive ($800+) but save time. When using a spool gun, set wire feed speed on the gun, not the machine. Keep the spool tension light so the wire doesn't birdnest. Use a contact tip one size larger than the wire, e.g., 1.2mm tip for 1.0mm wire. Clean the drive rolls regularly; aluminium wire leaves residue. In dusty environments, cover the spool when not in use. For both systems, use a liner made for aluminium, like a Teflon or nylon liner. Never use a steel liner; it will shave the wire. If you use a push-pull, adjust the tension so the wire doesn't slip but isn't crushed. Test by feeding wire onto a piece of wood; it should come out straight, not coiled. In Africa, where power can be unreliable, spool guns are often preferred because they draw less from the main feeder. But if you weld thick aluminium (over 6mm) regularly, invest in a push-pull. Always keep spare contact tips, nozzles, and drive rolls. A typical spool gun kit includes a spare tip and nozzle. Practice feeding wire without welding to get the feel. Remember, the gun should be held at a slight angle, and you should not drag the spool gun; push it forward.

lessons.title: Wire Types and Diameters
lessons.body: Choosing the right aluminium wire is critical. The most common wires are 4043 and 5356. 4043 (5% silicon) is softer, feeds better, and gives a shiny weld. It's great for general fabrication and castings. 5356 (5% magnesium) is stronger, harder, and feeds worse but gives better corrosion resistance and anodising colour match. For African workshops, 4043 is often the go-to because it's easier to find and cheaper. Wire diameters: 0.8mm, 1.0mm, and 1.2mm. For thin aluminium (1-3mm), use 0.8mm or 1.0mm. For thicker sections (3-6mm), use 1.2mm. The wire must match the base metal. For 6061, use 4043 or 5356. For 5052, use 5356. Never use steel wire in an aluminium MIG. Store wire in a dry place; moisture causes porosity. Buy wire from a reputable supplier; cheap wire often has inconsistent diameter, causing feed issues. In Africa, you can find 4043 wire at welding supply shops in major cities, but in rural areas, you may need to order online. A 1kg spool of 1.0mm 4043 costs about $15-$20. A 0.5kg spool for a spool gun costs $10-$15. Check the wire for bends or kinks before loading. If the wire is rusty or dirty, discard it. Use a wire cutter to snip the end at a 45-degree angle before feeding. Set drive roll tension so the wire deforms slightly but doesn't flatten. For 1.2mm wire, use a 1.4mm contact tip. For 1.0mm wire, use a 1.2mm tip. Keep a log of your settings for each wire type and thickness. Practice on scrap of the same alloy. If you get porosity, try a different wire or clean the base metal better. Remember, aluminium wire work-hardens if bent repeatedly, so avoid sharp bends in the liner. When switching from steel to aluminium, change the liner, drive rolls, and contact tip. Never mix.

lessons.title: Shielding Gas Selection
lessons.body: For MIG welding aluminium, you need 100% argon. Argon provides good cleaning action and stable arc. Do not use CO2 or argon-CO2 mixes; they cause black soot and poor welds. In Africa, argon is available in cylinders from suppliers like Afrox, BOC, or local gas companies. A typical cylinder is 10-20 litres, filled to 200 bar. Rent or buy a cylinder; refills cost about $50-$80. Flow rate: 12-18 litres per minute (LPM). Too low, and you get porosity; too high, and you get turbulence that draws in air. Use a flowmeter, not just a regulator. For thick aluminium (over 6mm), you can use a helium-argon mix (25-75% helium) to get more heat and better penetration. Helium is expensive and less common in Africa, but some suppliers stock it. If you use helium mix, increase flow rate to 20-25 LPM. Always purge the line before welding: open the valve, set flow, and let gas run for 5 seconds. Check for leaks with soapy water. In windy conditions, use a windbreak; even a slight breeze can blow away shielding gas. For outdoor work, increase flow to 20 LPM and use a larger nozzle. Keep the nozzle clean; spatter can block gas flow. Replace the nozzle if it's damaged. Use a gas lens kit for better coverage. In rural areas, you may need to transport cylinders carefully; secure them upright. Never use a cylinder without a regulator. When finished, close the cylinder valve and bleed the line. Store cylinders in a cool, ventilated area. If you run out of argon, don't substitute with CO2; stop and get argon. Practice on scrap to see the effect of flow rate: start at 12 LPM, then 18 LPM, and note the weld appearance. You want a clean, shiny bead with no porosity. If you see black spots, increase flow or check for leaks. Remember, argon is heavier than air, so it settles; in a pit, ensure ventilation.

lessons.title: Machine Settings
lessons.body: Setting your MIG machine for aluminium is about balancing voltage and wire feed speed. Start with the manufacturer's chart, but fine-tune by ear and eye. For 3mm aluminium, set voltage at 20-22V and wire speed at 6-8 m/min (or 300-400 inches per minute). For 6mm, use 23-25V and 8-10 m/min. For 1.5mm, use 17-19V and 4-6 m/min. These are starting points; adjust based on your machine. Use the 'sizzle' test: a steady frying sound means good. If it pops, increase voltage or decrease wire speed. If it stubs, increase voltage or decrease wire speed. If it burns through, decrease voltage or increase travel speed. Set the inductance (if available) to a medium-high setting for smoother arc. For spool guns, set wire speed on the gun. For push-pull, set on the main feeder. Always check polarity: DCEP (electrode positive) for aluminium. Some machines have a switch; set it to MIG. Use a contact tip one size larger than wire. Stick-out: 10-15mm. Travel angle: push 10-15 degrees. Travel speed: about 30-40 cm/min for 3mm. For a fillet weld, aim the wire at the root. For butt welds, leave a small gap (0-1mm) for penetration. Practice on scrap of the same thickness. Keep a notebook with settings for each job. In Africa, voltage fluctuations can affect settings; use a stabiliser or generator with AVR. If your machine has a digital display, note the numbers. If not, mark the dials. Always test on scrap before welding the actual part. Clean the base metal with a stainless brush. Preheating thick aluminium (over 10mm) to 100-150Â°C helps. Use a temperature crayon or infrared thermometer. After welding, clean the weld with a stainless brush and water to remove smut. Remember, aluminium welds cool fast; don't quench. Let it air cool. If you get porosity, check gas flow, wire cleanliness, and base metal. If you get cracks, try 5356 wire or preheat. Practice makes perfect.

lessons.title: Running Beads and Common Faults
lessons.body: Running a bead on aluminium requires steady hands and correct settings. Start with a push angle (forehand) of 10-15 degrees. Keep a consistent travel speed. For a straight bead on 3mm plate, use 20V, 6 m/min wire speed, and 15 LPM argon. The bead should be smooth with fine ripples. If you see a ropey bead, your travel speed is too fast or voltage too low. If the bead is too wide and flat, voltage is too high or travel too slow. Common faults: 1) Porosity (holes in weld) â caused by low gas flow, dirty wire, or moisture. Fix: increase gas to 15-18 LPM, clean wire, use fresh spool. 2) Burn-through â too much heat. Fix: reduce voltage, increase travel speed, use thicker material or backing. 3) Spatter â too much voltage or wrong gas. Fix: use 100% argon, reduce voltage. 4) Wire stubbing â wire hits plate and stops. Fix: increase voltage or decrease wire speed. 5) Birdnesting â wire tangles at drive rolls. Fix: reduce drive roll tension, use Teflon liner, don't kink wire. 6) Lack of fusion â travel too fast or voltage too low. Fix: slow down, increase voltage. 7) Cracking â wrong wire or too much restraint. Fix: use 5356 wire, preheat, or redesign joint. 8) Black smut â normal on aluminium; clean with stainless brush and water. For practice, run beads on scrap, then cut and etch to see penetration. In Africa, use a hacksaw and file to cut, then dip in caustic soda (careful!) to etch. Always wear PPE. If you get a fault, adjust one variable at a time. Keep a log. Watch videos of skilled welders to see technique. Practice daily for at least 30 minutes. Remember, aluminium welding is less forgiving than steel, but with patience, you can master it. Start with thin material and work up. Use a grinder to clean up bad welds and try again. Don't be afraid to ask for help from experienced welders in your area.

quiz.q: What polarity is used for MIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: DCEP (electrode positive) provides better cleaning action and penetration for aluminium.

quiz.q: Which shielding gas is correct for MIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: 100% argon gives the best cleaning action and stable arc for aluminium.

quiz.q: What is the recommended argon flow rate for MIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: 12-18 litres per minute provides adequate shielding without turbulence.

quiz.q: Which wire type is softer and feeds better for general aluminium fabrication?
quiz.explanation: 4043 (5% silicon) is softer and feeds more easily than 5356.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of porosity in aluminium MIG welds?
quiz.explanation: Low gas flow allows air to contaminate the weld, causing porosity.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a spool gun?
options: B) To feed soft aluminium wire over a short distance
D) To preheat the base metal
quiz.explanation: A spool gun mounts the wire spool on the gun, eliminating long feed distances that cause buckling.

quiz.q: Which liner material is recommended for aluminium wire?
quiz.explanation: Teflon or nylon liners reduce friction and prevent shaving of soft aluminium wire.

quiz.q: What is the correct contact tip size for 1.0mm aluminium wire?
quiz.explanation: Use a contact tip one size larger (1.2mm) to prevent binding of the soft wire.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stick-out for aluminium MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: 10-15mm stick-out provides good arc stability and gas coverage.

quiz.q: What is the correct travel angle for MIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Pushing (forehand) at 10-15 degrees gives better cleaning action and bead appearance.

quiz.q: Which wire type provides better corrosion resistance and anodising colour match?
quiz.explanation: 5356 (5% magnesium) offers better corrosion resistance and matches anodised colour better than 4043.

quiz.q: What is a common fix for wire birdnesting?
quiz.explanation: Too much drive roll tension crushes the soft wire, causing birdnesting; reduce tension.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get burn-through on thin aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Increasing travel speed reduces heat input, preventing burn-through.

quiz.q: Which gas mix can be used for thicker aluminium to increase heat?
quiz.explanation: Argon-helium mixes provide higher heat input for better penetration on thick aluminium.

quiz.q: What is the recommended preheat temperature for thick aluminium (over 10mm)?
quiz.explanation: Preheating to 100-150Â°C helps prevent cracking and improves fusion on thick sections.

quiz.q: What causes a ropey bead in aluminium MIG welding?
options: C) Travel speed too fast or voltage too low
quiz.explanation: A ropey bead indicates insufficient heat or too fast travel, so slow down or increase voltage.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to clean aluminium before welding?
options: B) Use a stainless steel brush
C) Use a wire brush on a drill
quiz.explanation: A stainless steel brush removes aluminium oxide without contaminating the surface.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a push-pull system?
options: A) To push wire from the machine and pull from the torch
B) To mix two shielding gases
quiz.explanation: A push-pull system has a motor in the torch that pulls wire while the main feeder pushes, allowing longer feed distances.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of lack of fusion in aluminium MIG welding?
options: C) Travel speed too fast or voltage too low
quiz.explanation: Lack of fusion occurs when heat input is insufficient, often due to fast travel or low voltage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see black smut on an aluminium weld?
options: B) Clean it with a stainless brush and water
quiz.explanation: Black smut is normal surface contamination; clean it with a stainless brush and water.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended practice for storing aluminium wire?
options: A) Keep in a dry place
quiz.explanation: Moisture causes porosity, so wire should be kept dry and sealed.

quiz.q: What is the typical wire feed speed for 3mm aluminium at 20-22V?
quiz.explanation: 6-8 m/min matches the voltage for a stable arc on 3mm aluminium.

quiz.q: What is the correct drive roll tension for aluminium wire?
options: B) Light tension so wire deforms slightly
D) Medium tension with visible flattening
quiz.explanation: Light tension prevents crushing the soft wire while still feeding it reliably.

quiz.q: What is the recommended nozzle type for better gas coverage?
quiz.explanation: A gas lens provides more laminar gas flow for better shielding.

quiz.q: What should you do if your wire stubs into the plate?
options: C) Increase voltage or decrease wire speed
quiz.explanation: Stubbing means insufficient heat, so increase voltage or reduce wire speed.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to cut aluminium wire before feeding?
quiz.explanation: A 45-degree cut helps the wire feed smoothly through the liner and tip.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of too much gas flow?
quiz.explanation: Excessive gas flow causes turbulence that draws in air, leading to porosity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct setting for 6mm aluminium?
quiz.explanation: 23-25V and 8-10 m/min provide adequate heat for 6mm aluminium.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of preheating aluminium?
options: B) To prevent cracking and improve fusion
quiz.explanation: Preheating reduces thermal gradient, preventing cracking and improving penetration.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get a birdnest at the drive rolls?
options: B) Reduce drive roll tension and check liner
quiz.explanation: Birdnesting is often caused by too much tension or a worn liner; reduce tension and inspect liner.
